attempts.raw_response: St. Brigid, for instance, in her Life by Cogitosus, is depicted as calling down divine vengeance upon a certain leper who dared to demand payment for water she had miraculously provided. The curse proved spectacularly effective, if the text is to be believed. Similarly, St. Mel of Ardagh is recorded as having pronounced doom upon a group of uncharitable nuns who refused to share their provisions with a poor traveler. The women were subsequently struck blind—a fate that seems somewhat disproportionate to the offense, yet illustrates the hagiographer's conviction that even the most meek and holy women possessed a formidable spiritual authority that could bend the divine will to punish the impious. These passages reveal that the power of malediction was considered no less real for being wielded by those whom the world might deem gentle.

pair.human_continuation:
St. Laisrech, for instance, condemned the
lands of those who refused her tribute, to--nettles, elder shrub, and
corncrakes!  It is pretty plain that the compilers of the lives had some
prerogatives, claims or rights to uphold--hence this frequent insistence
on the evil of resisting the Saint and presumably his successors.

One characteristic of the Irish ascetics appears very clear through all
the exaggeration and all the biographical absurdity; it is their spirit
of intense mortification.  To understand this we have only to study one
of the ancient Irish Monastic Rules or one of the Irish Penitentials as
edited by D'Achery ("Spicilegium") or Wasserschleben ("Irische
Kanonensamerlung"). Severest fasting, unquestioning obedience and
perpetual self renunciation were inculcated by the Rules and we have
ample evidence that they were observed with extraordinary fidelity.
pair.prefix:
In the text we shall see St. Mochuda, whose Life is a specially
sane piece of work, cursing on the same occasion, first, King Blathmac
and the Prince of Cluain, then, the rich man Cronan who sympathised with
the eviction, next an individual named Dubhsulach who winked insolently
at him, and finally the people of St. Columba's holy city of Durrow who
had stirred up hostile feeling against him. Even gentle female saints
can hurl an imprecation too.
